title: Hairy Skin, Stroking and Affective Touch

generated.pipeline: extract → Codex draft → Codex accuracy gate + fix (fresh context)

cards.front: A {{c1::low-threshold mechanoreceptor}} is a sensory neuron that responds to gentle mechanical force.
cards.quote: A low-threshold mechanoreceptor (LTMR) is a sensory neuron that responds to gentle mechanical force.

cards.front: An {{c1::afferent}} carries sensory signals toward the spinal cord and brain.
cards.quote: An afferent is any sensory fibre carrying signals toward the spinal cord and brain.

cards.front: Why does a human C-tactile afferent conduct slowly compared with fast touch afferents in hairy skin?
cards.back: Its thin C-fibre axon lacks insulating myelin; the fast touch afferents have myelinated axons.
cards.quote: A C-tactile (CT) afferent is a human LTMR with a thin, unmyelinated C-fibre axon, so it conducts slowly.

cards.front: What does microneurography record during controlled stimulation in an awake person?
cards.back: Single axons in a peripheral nerve, using a fine electrode passed through the skin.
cards.quote: In microneurography, a fine electrode is passed through the skin into a peripheral nerve to record single axons

cards.front: Human forearm CT afferents fire most strongly at brush speeds of about {{c1::1 to 10 cm/s}}.
cards.quote: The CT afferents' firing traced an inverted U, highest for strokes between about 1 and 10 cm/s and lower on either side.
cards.section: The fibre that prefers a caress

cards.front: What distinguishes the velocity tuning of human forearm CT afferents from that of the recorded myelinated touch afferents?
cards.back: CT firing rises then falls with speed; myelinated firing rises. The distinction is tuning shape, not a higher absolute CT firing rate.
cards.quote: The tuning, not a higher absolute firing rate, set CT afferents apart.
cards.section: The fibre that prefers a caress

cards.front: Suppose a pleasantness rating reads only touch fibres whose firing rises with brush speed, always interpreting more firing as more pleasant. What happens as speed increases, and why?
cards.back: Ratings rise with speed because the readout preserves the rising firing response. An intermediate-speed rating peak would contradict this simple readout.
cards.quote: read out in any way that keeps "more firing" meaning "more pleasant", ratings would also rise with speed.
cards.section: The fibre that prefers a caress

cards.front: Two groups provide matching curves: one group supplies sensory-fibre firing measurements and another supplies pleasantness ratings. What relationship does this establish?
cards.back: A correspondence between tuning curves, without showing that the recorded input is necessary or the only input to pleasantness.
cards.quote: The ratings and the recordings came from different people, so the 2009 result is a correspondence between two tuning curves.
cards.section: The fibre that prefers a caress

cards.front: A brain circuit subtracts a steadily rising touch signal from one that rises quickly and then saturates. Could its output peak at intermediate speeds without an intermediate-tuned input, and why?
cards.back: Yes. Rule: a rapidly rising, saturating signal minus a continually rising signal can peak in the middle. Thus matching an output peak to one afferent class does not uniquely identify its cause.
cards.quote: a signal that rises quickly and levels off, minus one that keeps rising, also peaks in the middle.
cards.section: The fibre that prefers a caress

cards.front: Two people receive the same caress-speed forearm stroke but differ in who they believe is touching them. Must they give identical pleasantness ratings, and why?
cards.back: No. Group-average velocity tuning does not determine an individual rating; who is touching, the situation and brain processing also influence pleasantness.
cards.quote: which also depends on who is touching, on the situation and on processing in the brain.
cards.section: The fibre that prefers a caress

cards.front: What did pleasant hairy-skin sensation in the patient lacking large myelinated afferents show about CT input?
cards.back: CT input can support a faint, pleasant sensation without large myelinated afferents. This does not establish that CT input is necessary.
cards.quote: The case shows what CT input can do without large myelinated afferents, not that it is needed.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: HSAN-V carriers with reduced thin-fibre density rated slow arm stroking as less pleasant than controls. Why is this not a selective test of CT necessity?
cards.back: The mutation reduces more fibres than CT afferents alone. The result supports a thin-fibre contribution without isolating CT input.
cards.quote: the mutation affects more fibres than CT afferents alone, so it is not a clean removal of CT input.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: How did anterolateral cordotomy affect pain, temperature, itch and brush pleasantness in the human study?
cards.back: Pain, temperature and itch were markedly disrupted; brush pleasantness ratings were not significantly changed.
cards.quote: It did not: pain, temperature and itch were markedly disrupted, but pleasantness ratings were not significantly changed.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: Why do pleasantness ratings surviving anterolateral cordotomy constrain the route model without proving the cut had zero effect?
cards.back: Survival rules out that tract as the sole obligatory route. A nonsignificant change in 19 patients does not prove that no change occurred.
cards.quote: With 19 patients, "not significantly changed" is not proof of no change, but ratings that did not vanish rule out the anterolateral tract as the one obligatory route.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: After a sensory-pathway intervention, people still detect light contact but rate texture and stroke intensity lower. What additional measure tests whether touch pleasantness was also lost?
cards.back: Measure brush pleasantness separately before and after the intervention. Rule: detection, intensity, texture and pleasantness can dissociate. Changes in the first three do not establish a change in the fourth.
cards.quote: ratings of stroking intensity and of texture fell, while monofilament detection thresholds were spared.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: How can reduced pleasantness with thin-fibre loss coexist with pleasantness surviving anterolateral cordotomy, and what remains unknown?
cards.back: Rule: removing input and cutting one route test different questions. Thin-fibre input could contribute while information survives through another route. Neither result identifies whether the surviving information comes from CT afferents, Aβ afferents or both.
cards.quote: Neither test shows which fibres carry the signal that survives the cut: CT afferents, Aβ afferents or both together.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: On a log velocity axis, equal distances represent equal {{c1::ratios}} of speed.
cards.quote: On a log axis, equal distances are equal ratios of speed:
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: For the pre-cordotomy group fit for the pain-affected side y = -2.07x² + 1.88x + 6.22, with x = log10(v in cm/s), calculate the velocity and rating at the fitted maximum.
cards.back: Set dy/dx = -4.14x + 1.88 = 0: x = 1.88/4.14 ≈ 0.4541. The second derivative is -4.14, confirming a maximum. Thus v = 10^x ≈ 2.85 cm/s and y ≈ 6.65.
cards.quote: y = -2.07x² + 1.88x + 6.22, where x = log10(v in cm/s), R² = 0.22
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: Using y = -2.07x² + 1.88x + 6.22 and x = log10(v in cm/s), calculate predicted pleasantness at the three tested speeds: 0.3, 3 and 30 cm/s.
cards.back: Substitute x = log10(v): x ≈ -0.523, 0.477 and 1.477, respectively. Evaluating the polynomial gives y ≈ 4.67, 6.65 and 4.48; the tested middle speed has the highest predicted rating.
cards.quote: the tested 0.3, 3 and 30 cm/s sit one tenfold step apart,
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: A quadratic fit to pleasantness at only 0.3, 3 and 30 cm/s peaks at 2.85 cm/s. Would it establish that 2.85 cm/s is preferred over 3 cm/s, and why?
cards.back: No. The exact peak is imposed by the parabolic interpolation between tested speeds. Additional measurements near the fitted peak would be needed to resolve that preference.
cards.quote: The shape between the tested speeds, including the exact 2.85 cm/s peak, comes from assuming a parabola.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: A pleasantness fit has R² = 0.22 but already passes through each tested speed's mean rating. Would changing only the curve in velocity explain more variance on those same data, and why?
cards.back: No. A curve already passing through the speed means cannot do better on those data. The remaining variance lies among ratings at the same speed, much of it differences between patients.
cards.quote: Because the curve already passes through the averages, no curve in velocity could do better on these data.
cards.section: Take the input away: what people show

cards.front: What endings did identified TH-positive mouse C-LTMRs have in the ex vivo recordings?
cards.back: Lanceolate endings running lengthwise along zigzag and awl/auchene hair follicles.
cards.quote: Their endings were lanceolate: nerve terminals that run lengthwise along a hair follicle, parallel to the hair shaft.
cards.section: Which cells detect a stroke in mice

cards.front: What did the original genetic tracing establish about mouse MrgprB4 fibres?
cards.back: They were unmyelinated, nonpeptidergic fibres innervating hairy skin only; the study was anatomical, without a tactile response recording.
cards.quote: The fibres were unmyelinated and nonpeptidergic and innervated hairy skin only.
cards.section: Which cells detect a stroke in mice

cards.front: Mouse Aβ field-LTMR endings are {{c1::circumferential}}, wrapping around rather than running along hair follicles.
cards.quote: whose endings are circumferential: they wrap around the follicle instead of running along it.
cards.section: Which cells detect a stroke in mice

cards.front: A mouse Aβ field-LTMR ignores movement of a single hair. If a gentle brush moves many of its follicles together, what response is predicted, and why?
cards.back: It can fire. The proposed mechanism is summation across many weakly sensitive endings, allowing a stroke to reach threshold even when one hair cannot.
cards.quote: the neuron sums many weakly sensitive endings, so a stroke that moves many follicles at once reaches threshold when no single hair can.
cards.section: Which cells detect a stroke in mice

cards.front: MrgprB4 terminal activity was recorded during mouse stroking at about 0.5 to 2 cm/s. Would using that band in a new experiment establish the mouse optimal speed, and why?
cards.back: No. That range was the tested protocol, not a measured optimum. A velocity tuning measurement is needed; the human preferred band of about 1 to 10 cm/s cannot simply be transferred.
cards.quote: That is the protocol's speed, not an estimate of the mouse optimum, and the human 1 to 10 cm/s band should not be carried across.
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: How should conditioned place preference after MrgprB4 activation in young male mice be interpreted?
cards.back: The authors interpreted activation as reinforcing, anxiolytic or both in that assay. It tests sufficiency for the outcome, without proving necessity or reporting pleasure.
cards.quote: The authors read the preference as positive reinforcement, anxiolysis (reduced anxiety) or both, and kept both readings open.
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: A developmental Mrgprb4 lineage includes cells with {{c1::past}} marker expression, not just cells expressing it in adulthood.
cards.quote: permanently switches on a label in cells that recombined after expressing Mrgprb4 at some point, and in their descendants,
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: What behavioural outcomes followed optogenetic activation of Mrgprb4-lineage afferents in adult female mouse back skin?
cards.back: Place preference and lordosis-like dorsiflexion, a posture resembling that of a receptive female during mating. These are measured behaviours, not reports of feeling.
cards.quote: activation of these afferents in back skin produced place preference and a dorsiflexion resembling lordosis,
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: Developmental Mrgprb4-lineage ablation reduced adult female receptivity and the accumbens dopamine-sensor signal during mounting. Does this establish that adult Mrgprb4-expressing neurons are needed for pleasure?
cards.back: No. Developmental lineage loss does not isolate cells expressing the marker in adulthood or exclude developmental effects. Receptivity and a dopamine-sensor signal are behavioural and neural readouts, not measurements of pleasure.
cards.quote: Ablating the lineage, a removal that began during development, reduced sexual receptivity in the adults.
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: CaV3.2 deletion in the Nav1.8 lineage reduced mouse social and tactile interactions. Can this result be assigned exclusively to C-LTMR dysfunction, and why?
cards.back: No. The developmental deletion was not confined to C-LTMRs because the Nav1.8 lineage includes other neurons.
cards.quote: Nav1.8 is not restricted to C-LTMRs, so the deletion was not confined to them.
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: Reducing Tac1-neuron activity in the mouse periaqueductal gray abolished touch-evoked PVH oxytocin-neuron firing. What does this identify, and what peripheral claim remains untested?
cards.back: It identifies a central requirement for that touch-evoked firing. It does not identify which peripheral touch afferents are needed or establish a role for Mrgprb4 neurons.
cards.quote: Reducing Tac1-neuron activity abolished the touch-evoked oxytocin firing.
cards.section: From skin to reward-like outcomes in mice

cards.front: Why should TH-positive mouse C-LTMRs and MrgprB4 neurons not be treated as interchangeable candidates for human CT afferents?
cards.back: They are different populations: TH-positive C-LTMRs do not express MrgprB4. Neither has been conclusively matched to physiologically identified human CT afferents.
cards.quote: TH-positive C-LTMRs do not express MrgprB4, so the two are different populations,
cards.section: Which mouse neuron is a CT afferent, and what "pleasant" can mean in a mouse

cards.front: A Mrgprb4 developmental lineage responds to pressure and temperature. Must adult Mrgprb4-expressing neurons have both responses, and why?
cards.back: No. Developmental lineage labelling includes a broader progenitor-derived population; mixed lineage responses need not describe the adult marker-defined neurons.
cards.quote: the lineage is broader than the adult population, because Mrgprb4 expression starts in a broader set of progenitors,
cards.section: Which mouse neuron is a CT afferent, and what "pleasant" can mean in a mouse

cards.front: Mouse marker-defined neurons respond to stroking and support place preference. What evidence would bridge them to human CT afferents, rather than equating shared responses with cell identity?
cards.back: Link molecular profiles to physiologically identified human CT units and compare the resulting identity with mouse types. Rule: mouse markers or behavioural proxies cannot establish the human counterpart; human molecular data must be tied to recorded units.
cards.quote: Settling the match needs human molecular data tied to physiologically identified units, and that work has begun
cards.section: Which mouse neuron is a CT afferent, and what "pleasant" can mean in a mouse

cards.front: Design access to adult Mrgprb4-expressing neurons that avoids labelling the whole developmental lineage. What validation and control are needed?
cards.back: Use a validated inducible Mrgprb4 driver, if available, and induce it in adults. Confirm labelled ganglion cells with a reporter and include induced mice lacking the driver. Rule: adult marker expression and developmental lineage can differ.
cards.quote: Confirm recombination in the ganglia with a reporter and check which cells are labelled, since the lineage and the adult population may differ.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Activation of a touch-neuron population produces place preference. Design a separate test of whether it is needed for touch reward using a comparable outcome.
cards.back: Silence or ablate the population in adults, then measure touch-conditioned place preference against controls. Rule: activation tests sufficiency; loss of function tests necessity. Use the same reward readout for the two arms.
cards.quote: then test touch-conditioned place preference, the same reward readout the sufficiency arm uses.
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: Why measure locomotion and posture when a touch-neuron manipulation changes a mating receptivity readout?
cards.back: A motor or postural change could be mistaken for altered receptivity. Those measurements help distinguish the explanations.
cards.quote: Measure locomotion and posture so a motor change is not read as receptivity,
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: If neurons respond to stroking and temperature and are required for place preference, why does this not establish a dedicated pleasant-touch line?
cards.back: Their responses span modalities. Necessity for a measured behaviour establishes neither touch specificity nor a report of pleasure.
cards.quote: If they respond to more than touch, call the result "required for this behaviour," not "a pleasure line."
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How does finding a few CT afferents in human glabrous hand skin change the scope of the hairy-skin model?
cards.back: CT afferents are sparse rather than absent there. Hairy-skin results cannot simply be generalized to glabrous skin; the density estimate rests on only three recorded units.
cards.quote: recorded three CT afferents in human glabrous hand skin, about 1 for every 80 myelinated mechanoreceptors recorded,
cards.section: Glabrous skin: sparse, not absent
